3. A test set W = w_1 w_2 (N = 2 words) has model probabilities P(w_1) = 1/2 and P(w_2) = 1/8. What is the perplexity PP(W)? Assume the word choices are conditionally independent.
4. Word embeddings (e.g., from Word2Vec or the embedding layer of an LLM) are useful primarily because they:
options: Reduce all words to a single scalar value
Guarantee zero probability for unseen words
Represent words as dense vectors capturing semantic and syntactic similarity
Eliminate the need for training data
questions.correctAnswer: Represent words as dense vectors capturing semantic and syntactic similarity
questions.explanation: Embeddings map words to dense continuous vectors so that semantically and syntactically related words lie close together in vector space, unlike sparse one-hot representations.

questions.question: 5. In a corpus, the bigram "and the" occurs 2 times, the unigram "and" occurs 48 times, and the vocabulary size is V = 500. Under Add-1 smoothing, P("the" | "and") is approximately:

6. Consider the training corpus (with sentence boundaries):
<s> the cat runs </s>
<s> the dog runs </s>
<s> the cat sleeps </s>

Using MLE, what is the bigram probability P(cat | the)?
questions.explanation: "the" occurs 3 times. It is followed by "cat" twice and "dog" once. P(cat | the) = count(the, cat) / count(the) = 2/3.

questions.question: 7. What is the effect of Add-1 smoothing on the relative probabilities of a frequent word pair versus an infrequent word pair?
options: It widens the gap between their probabilities
It narrows (compresses) the gap between their probabilities, moving both toward a more uniform distribution
It leaves all relative probabilities unchanged
It sets both probabilities exactly equal
questions.correctAnswer: It narrows (compresses) the gap between their probabilities, moving both toward a more uniform distribution
questions.explanation: By uniformly adding 1 to every count, Add-1 smoothing takes a large amount of probability mass from high-count pairs and gives it to low/zero-count pairs, compressing the gap between frequent and infrequent pairs (it can over-smooth).

questions.question: 8. In corpus C, the bigram probability P(paper | question) = 0.25 and count("question") = 800. If the vocabulary size is V = 1000, what is P(paper | question) after Add-1 smoothing?
questions.explanation: C(question, paper) = P(paper | question) * C(question) = 0.25 * 800 = 200. P_Add-1(paper | question) = (C(w_1, w_2) + 1) / (C(w_1) + V) = (200 + 1) / (800 + 1000) = 201 / 1800 ≈ 0.112.

questions.question: 9. Why do unigram models perform especially poorly in the Shannon "predict the next word" game (e.g., "For breakfast I ate my usual ___")?
options: Because unigrams require the entire vocabulary to be labeled
Because unigrams ignore all preceding words and predict based only on individual word frequencies
Because unigrams cannot assign probabilities at all
questions.correctAnswer: Because unigrams ignore all preceding words and predict based only on individual word frequencies
questions.explanation: A unigram model assigns probabilities to words independent of context. Since it ignores the preceding words entirely, it cannot use the context that makes the next word predictable, so it is terrible at next-word prediction.

questions.question: 10. A unigram language model that treats all words as equally likely achieves a perplexity of 100 on a test set. What is the probability the model assigns to each individual word?
questions.explanation: For equal probabilities, perplexity PP(W) = V = 100. The probability assigned to each individual word is P(w) = 1 / V = 1 / 100 = 0.01.
